title: Developing a daily life measure of depression for persons with aphasia and examining its relation with communicative confidence
text:
The proposed study focuses on developing and validating a daily life measure of
depression for persons with aphasia and investigating its association with
communicative confidence. Results will contribute to new evidence regarding the
validity of a daily-life measure of depression and its relationship with communicative
confidence. An accurate identification of depression in persons with aphasia in their
natural environment can lead to real-time depression interventions which can ultimately
improve their daily life.

title: Postsynaptic roles of ankyrins
text:
While conventionally seen as restricted to axon initial segments, recent evidence has implicated Ankyrin-G
and Ankyrin-B in the biology of central nervous system glutamatergic synapses. However, little is known
about their postsynaptic roles. Here, building on our progress made during the previous funding period, we
will investigate the functions of ankyrins and their protein partners at cortical glutamatergic synapses,
cortical circuits, and behaviors controlled by the frontal cortex.

title: Molecular Genetics Resource Core
text: Molecular Genetics Resource Core Project Summary The Molecular Genetics Resource Core (MGRC) will provide a variety of services for the University of Washington Center for Excellence in Opioid Research. We will provide state-of-the-art viral vectors for neural circuit dissection, generate numerous viral-based CRISPR/Cas9 targeting vectors for in vivo molecular circuit analysis, and provide access to platforms for the viral delivery of novel sensors and actuators developed by UW addiction researchers. The NIDA-P30 MGRC will also generate novel mouse lines for UW addiction researchers and provide access to existing mouse lines for researcher-initiated investigations. A major provision of the NIDA-P30 MGRC will be hands on training in molecular genetics techniques for graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and qualified undergraduates. We will also provide a Summer Workshop for the education and training of UW addiction research trainees. Collectively the resources, education, and training provided by the NIDA-P30 MGRC will facilitate the rapid dissemination of cutting-edge research on the molecular and genetic basis of opioid addiction and prepare the next generation of scientists for careers in substance use disorder research.

title: Function of astrocytic NMDA receptors
text:
NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function is essential for normal neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity necessary for
learning and memory and NMDARs represent important therapeutic targets for neurological and neuropsychiatric
disorders. Recent studies have identified expression of NMDARs in non-neuronal cells including astrocytes but their
function in these cells is poorly understood. The proposed studies will characterize the properties and function of
astrocytic NMDARs and their role in regulating synaptic function and NMDA channel blocker effects in brain regions
relevant to pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Mechanistic modeling to determine demographic, behavioral, and environmental factors that facilitate or prevent influenza transmission in households
text: Project Summary – Project 3 Despite decades of influenza research into host- and virus-based drivers of infectivity and susceptibility, there remains a considerable gap in our understanding of how the community and household environmental contexts surrounding transmission perpetuate seasonal outbreaks. Individual and household factors such as behavioral patterns, degree of exposure to the community, the household built environment, and indoor air characteristics contribute to infection risk in ways that transcend elements of immunity and virology. The long-term goal of this research is to achieve a mechanistic understanding of human influenza transmission through the modeling of rich datasets collected from household studies. The core objectives of this project are to examine demographic, behavioral, and environmental factors that facilitate or prevent influenza transmission in households, using combined data from multiple household studies. For our proposed study, we will leverage a modern body of observational studies based at the University of Michigan since 2010 that were inspired by the Tecumseh studies, benefitting from improved laboratory assays and innovative sampling methodologies. Specifically, we will take advantage of existing and newly collected data from two prospective household cohort studies and a case- ascertained study. We will use state-of-the-art techniques including data augmentation and stochastic household transmission models to estimate key transmission parameters. We will address key knowledge gaps in human influenza transmission in three specific aims: (Aim 1) Determine the relative contributions of community-to- household and within-household transmission to influenza and other respiratory virus infections. We will use advanced data augmentation approaches to impute the daily infectious status of household members and apply a household transmission model to estimate transmission parameters for influenza and other respiratory viruses. (Aim 2) Determine individual drivers (demographic, behavioral, and infection/vaccination history) of influenza transmission, both from the infected individual and to the exposed individual. Building on the approach developed in Aim 1, we will augment our model with parameters for individual characteristics of both those who are infected and those who are susceptible to build a better understanding of who is driving influenza in the household, and how. (Aim 3) Determine shared household environmental drivers of influenza transmission. We will modify our household transmission model to account for characteristics of the household environment. This project is innovative because it will apply state-of-the-art transmission models to a large and rich dataset of influenza viruses in households. By advancing our understanding of the individual and household factors that contribute to human-to-human influenza transmission in real-world environments, this work will help to design meaningful and efficient mitigation strategies, thereby enhancing public health preparedness efforts.

title: Systems Genetics of Vascular Smooth Muscle Phenotypes
text:
Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in the United States. It manifests itself in the arteries and
can lead to myocardial infarction. Understanding the biological networks that underlie the complex interactions
in coronary artery disease is required for disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

title: Enhancing Multi-User Nucleic Acid Research Capabilities Through Acquisition of a High-Throughput Oligonucleotide Synthesizer
text:
The Shasta Oligonucleotide Synthesizer will enable Pittsburgh-area researchers to advance biomedical
research by making specialized DNA and RNA molecules more accessible for therapeutic development.
This equipment will empower academic scientists and spur collaborations with industry to conduct
comprehensive screening studies testing hundreds of chemically-modified sequences - work essential for
discovering new treatments for cancer, rare diseases, and other serious health conditions, while reducing
costs by 90% and providing access to specialized chemical modifications unavailable commercially. This
infrastructure will accelerate the development of life-saving therapies and strengthen the region's capacity
for cutting-edge biomedical research.

title: P-Selectin-Targeting Nanoparticles to Potentiate Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
Our project leverages a novel nanoparticle platform to precisely deliver small molecules that target senescent
cells, significantly enhancing their therapeutic index. Building on extensive preliminary data, we aim to combine
this platform with immunotherapies to reverse the immunosuppressive microenvironment of solid tumors and
improve patient outcomes.

title: Modeling neuroendocrine bladder cancer for studying the pathogenesis and improving chemotherapy responses
text:
ROJECT NARRATIVE
Compared to conventional bladder cancer, neuroendocrine bladder cancer is a highly lethal disease with a
poor response to chemotherapy and no effective second-line treatment. To address the lack of robust model
systems for neuroendocrine bladder cancer, we have developed complementary preclinical models, including
genetically engineered neuroendocrine bladder models and patient-derived xenografts that replicate the same
altered pathways. This proposed research will utilize our novel mouse models and patient-derived xenografts
to uncover the distinct molecular mechanisms underlying neuroendocrine bladder cancer and to enhance the
efficacy of current standard-of-care chemotherapy.

title: Cross-species analysis of regulatory function using synthetic regulatory genomics
text:
Noncoding sequence variation underpins the majority of the genetics of common human diseases and traits.
This proposal investigates the function of human regulatory DNA in mouse cells, which will provide insight into
how transcriptional regulation functions in different contexts, and provide a basis for new disease models.

title: Statistical Power Analysis Framework for Multi-Sample and Cross-Platform Spatial Omics Experiments
text:
Newly emerging spatial omics experiments can promote our understanding of spatial and molecular patterns
and relevant biological mechanisms associated with various organs and diseases such as cancers and
neurodegenerative disorders. The proposed power analysis framework will help improving design of spatial
omics experiments, which in turn will help guarantee biologically meaningful findings. The high impact of this
framework will be reflected through an interactive web interface with a coding-free environment that will assist
basic scientists, clinical scientists, and bioinformaticians in their design of spatial omics experiments.

title: Characterizing germline determinants of tumor development and response to treatment
text:
There remains a critical gap in understanding how inherited genetic variations contribute to somatic alterations
and influence treatment response. In this proposal, we will re-analyze existing real-world cohorts with novel
computational approaches followed by functional validation to identify and characterize germline determinants
of tumor evolutionary pathways, treatment response and treatment-related adverse events. These studies will
broaden our understanding of cancer genetics and eventually lead to improved prevention and intervention
strategies.

title: Prenatal Alcohol Exposure and Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as an understanding of those molecular pathways that
modify sensitivity to prenatal alcohol exposure-induced birth defects is expected in the long-term to inform
clinical practice and ultimately reduce the incidence and severity of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD).
This objective will be met by applying two innovative and complementary approaches to assess in cell and
animal models if novel genes or chemicals modulate the deficits elicited by ethanol exposure. Thus, the
proposed research is relevant to the parts of NIH/NIAAA’s mission that pertains to characterizing biological
mechanisms underlying FASD, identifying biomarkers of prenatal alcohol exposure, and ultimately will reveal
fundamental and novel insights into the mechanism of ethanol-induced birth defects.

title: Dietary DHA mitigates ozone induced pulmonary inflammation
text:
This application will generate critical data needed to develop docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) as a dietary
intervention for lowering pulmonary inflammation in response to O3 exposure for the general public and those
with obesity. This line of research will impact the health of Americans that are at risk for pulmonary inflammation
by improving their diet quality.

title: Center for Bat One Health Investigations, Research, and Outbreak Response (CHIRO)
text:
Center for Bat One Health Investigations, Research, and Outbreak response (CHIRO)
Project Narrative
Bat populations worldwide are increasingly threatened by environmental and anthropogenic stressors, which can influence patterns of viral shedding, drive virus evolution, and lead to increased spillover and outbreaks in people. To address this need, the Center for Bat One Health Investigations, Research, and Outbreak response (CHIRO, for “Chiroptera”) will pair laboratory studies at the Chiropteran Research Facility at Colorado State University with field investigations on filovirus ecology in West Africa (Ghana, Nigeria), where various stressors are actively impacting reservoir bats in the genera Mops and Rousettus. CHIRO will implement the One Health framework to integrate these bat disease ecology studies with human surveillance to enhance outbreak
preparedness and protect human and wildlife health.

title: Cross-platform structural variant discovery with deep learning
text:
Deep learning shifts method development from hand-engineered models and pipelines to flexible models that can
achieve state-of-the-art performance and learn complex patterns directly from the data. In this proposal we aim to
leverage the potential of deep learning for the problem of SV discovery by developing a framework to call and genotype
germline and somatic SVs, including complex variants, using data from different sequencing platforms. Improving SV
detection will have a significant impact on our ability to characterize, diagnose, and treat a wide range of diseases driven
by SVs, such as cancer and numerous neurological, autoimmune, and cardiovascular disorders.

title: Synthetic biology core for vector construction and strain optimization
text:
Engineered Salmonella are a promising and novel bacterial cancer therapy for triple-negative breast cancer.
This research leverages new high-throughput approaches to efficiently optimize the bacterial cells for enhanced
tumor colonization, improved therapeutic index for bacterial theranostic radioimmunotherapy, and control of
immune response for antitumor efficacy. Results from these studies will generate datasets that uncover the
genetic basis of these enhanced bacterial traits and deliver optimized engineered Salmonella for synergistic
cancer treatment approaches.

title: University of Washington Biomedical Informatics and Data Science Research Training Program
text:
The research training program in Biomedical Informatics and Data Science at the University of Washington aims
to prepare future leaders who will unleash the potential for electronic biomedical data and information to advance
research and improve health. These future leaders will utilize informatics and data science approaches to
address the significant challenges in health care and biomedicine and will create innovations that will improve
health outcomes at the individual and population level.

title: Functional anatomy, physiology and behavioral responses mediated by mu opioid receptor signaling on medial thalamic neurons.
text:
Opioids like morphine act across many brain regions to regulate reward and pain processing; opioid-sensitive
thalamic neurons connect many of these brain regions. The focus of this work is to determine which thalamic
neurons are activated during hyperalgesia (increased pain sensitivity), whether opioids inhibit hyperalgesia-
activated neurons and whether inhibition of these thalamic neurons is sufficient to prevent hyperalgesia. These
results may help identify new strategies to dissociate the desired and undesired effects of opioids.

title: University of Virginia Cancer Center Support Grant
text: The mission of the University of Virginia Cancer Center (UVACC) is to eliminate the threat of cancer, with skilled, compassionate care for the patients of today and with research and education for the patients of the future. UVACC Members draw on the deep resources of the University of Virginia to identify, analyze, and validate some of the most significant targets for cancer therapy, diagnosis and prevention, and to speed their translation to clinical application for the benefit of the people of the catchment area and beyond.
